Learn how cardio load tracks your workout effort, and how to use target load to find a better workout routine

Cardio load measures how hard your heart works, from brisk walks to peak effort. Each minute your heart rate is at least 30% of your heart-rate reserve while you are moving earns load, and harder minutes earn exponentially more.\n\nYour daily target load is personalized from your cardio load over the past four weeks, your fitness target and your daily readiness. Hitting it regularly maintains your fitness; going above it from time to time builds fitness, but doing so too often raises the risk of overtraining.

Your Daily Readiness score ranges from 1–100 and helps you understand how ready you are to work out

Daily Readiness compares last night’s heart rate variability, your resting heart rate and your past week of sleep with your own 30-day baseline. Wear your device to sleep for at least a week to get a reliable score.

Low (1–29): prioritize recovery, with lighter exercise like stretching or yoga.
Moderate (30–64): your recovery signals are about usual; your body is balancing exercise and stress with recovery.
High (65–100): your body is well rested and recovered.

Moderate readiness indicates a healthy balance between exercise and recovery
Low readiness scores might suggest you’d benefit from more recovery time, or lighter workouts

Wear your device to track your heart rate
Your heart rate zones are personalised to your cardiovascular fitness and age
Being physically active is one way to keep your heart healthy. Heart health is an important part of your overall good health.

Your heart rate shows how hard your heart is working. A lower resting heart rate usually means a fitter heart, and regular time in the moderate zone and above strengthens it.\n\nopenFit reads the heart rate your device writes to Health Connect and places each minute in a zone based on your heart-rate reserve.

Resting heart rate is the number of times your heart beats per minute while you are still and well rested, usually measured while you sleep. For most adults it is between 60 and 100 bpm; fitter people tend to have lower rates. A rate well above your usual can be a sign of illness, stress or too little recovery.
openFit sets your zones from your heart-rate reserve (max heart rate 220 − age, minus your resting rate): moderate from 40 %, vigorous from 60 % and peak from 85 %. Below moderate is the light zone.

Sleep tracking uses body signals collected by your device to estimate your sleep metrics. Tracking sleep can help you better understand how well you feel when you’re awake.

Your device writes your sleep and its stages to Health Connect. openFit reads them to show your time asleep, a sleep timeline and a sleep score.\n\nThe sleep score adds up time asleep (up to 50 points), time in deep and REM sleep (up to 25) and how restful the night was, from the share of time awake (up to 25). 90+ is excellent, 80–89 good, 60–79 fair and below 60 poor.

Your sleep moves through stages several times a night. Light sleep makes up most of it; deep sleep supports physical recovery and REM sleep supports memory and mood. Waking briefly many times a night is normal.

Breathing rate is how many breaths you take a minute, averaged over your sleep. It usually stays steady from night to night, so a change away from your personal range can be worth noticing.

Resting heart rate is how fast your heart beats while you are still and rested. A lower number usually goes with better fitness; a rise above your range can follow stress, illness, alcohol or poor sleep.

Heart rate variability is the variation in time, in milliseconds, between your heartbeats while you sleep. Higher than usual often means your body is well recovered; lower than usual can follow hard training, stress or illness.

Blood oxygen (SpO2) estimates how much of your blood carries oxygen, measured while you sleep. It is normally a little lower asleep than awake. It needs a device that measures SpO2 and writes it to Health Connect.
Skin temp variation is how your skin temperature during sleep differs from your own baseline. It moves with your environment, your cycle and illness, so watch for changes that last several nights.
These metrics are not intended to diagnose or treat any medical condition. They help you notice changes in your own wellbeing; if you are concerned about your health, talk to a healthcare provider.

Your highest level each day, usually after sleep.
An estimate of your energy in reserve, from 1 to 100%. Sleep charges it; stress and workouts drain it.

Energy Bank moves every 6 minutes.
Asleep: a full 7.5-hour night charges about 40 points.
Awake and calm: when your heart rate sits low among your usual awake heart rates of the last 30 days, the bank charges a little.
Awake and stressed: a higher heart rate drains it, faster the higher it ranks; about 55 points over a waking day at middling stress. Workouts drain through the same heart rate.
Charging slows as the bank fills and draining as it empties, and the level carries over midnight. It shows after a week of wearing your device. The rates are tuned to match Pulse.
It is a model, not a measurement: it cannot see mental effort that leaves your heart rate unchanged, food or caffeine.

From %1$d of %2$d inputs over the last 28 days. The ones present stand for all nine.
Pulse Age compares you with people of your age and sex. Add both in your profile.
How old your body behaves, from nine habits and vitals compared with references for your age and sex.

Each input maps to a change in the risk of dying from any cause, against a reference for your age and sex, using published studies: VO2 max (Kodama 2009), resting heart rate (Zhang 2016), steps (Paluch 2022), sleep hours (Saint-Maurice 2024), sleep consistency (Windred 2024), moderate and vigorous minutes (Arem 2015, Ahmadi 2022), strength training (Momma 2022) and body fat (Jayedi 2022).

The changes add up and turn into years: about 5 years per unit of log hazard ratio, half the 10 a year of age implies, because separate studies overstate their joint effect. Inputs without data are left out and the ones present scaled up to stand for all nine; at least 5 are needed. Pulse Age stays within 15 years of your age.

Moderate minutes are openFit’s fat-burn and cardio zones, vigorous the peak zone. Strength counts strength, weight, calisthenics, HIIT, Pilates and yoga workouts.

It rests on population studies, not a clinical test of your body.

VO2 max is the most oxygen your body can use in hard exercise, in millilitres per kilogram of body weight per minute. The higher it is, the fitter your heart and lungs.
openFit uses a measured value when a watch or app has written one to Health Connect. Otherwise it estimates one from your resting heart rate over the last 30 days: 15.3 × maximum heart rate ÷ resting heart rate, with maximum heart rate 220 − age (Uth et al. 2004).
The bands compare you with people of your age and sex in the FRIEND treadmill registry (Kaminsky et al. 2015): Poor below the 20th percentile, then Fair, Good, Excellent, and Superior from the 80th.
